title: Boeing Q3 2026 Results: Revenue Rises 4% as Net Loss Narrows Sharply
excerpt: Revenue rose to $24.188 billion and the net loss narrowed to $116 million from $5.339 billion a year ago; core loss of $0.34 per share missed estimates as Commercial Airplanes stayed unprofitable.
body:
• Boeing's third-quarter revenue rose 4% year over year to $24.188 billion, roughly in line with estimates, while its net loss narrowed sharply to $116 million, or $0.26 per share, from a $5.339 billion loss a year earlier.
  • Core loss per share was $0.34, wider than the roughly $0.21 consensus loss; Commercial Airplanes lost $697 million, while Defense, Space & Security earned $492 million and Global Services earned $1.019 billion.
  • Boeing delivered 161 commercial airplanes in the quarter and ended it with a record $745 billion backlog, including more than 6,300 commercial airplanes valued at $612 billion.
  • Operating cash flow was $1.496 billion and free cash flow was $464 million despite about $700 million in Justice Department settlement payments; stabilizing 737 output at 47 per month is now expected to take until next year.

Boeing's third-quarter results on Tuesday showed a company climbing out of last year's deep losses but still short of profitability in its core jetliner business. Revenue rose, the headline loss narrowed dramatically — when a large 777X charge weighed on results a year ago — and defense and services carried the quarter, even as the commercial recovery took longer than planned.

Revenue rose 4% to $24.188 billion in the quarter ended September 30, from $23.270 billion a year earlier, according to the company's third-quarter release. Boeing swung to operating earnings of $354 million from a $4.781 billion operating loss, for a 1.5% operating margin. The net loss narrowed to $116 million, or $0.26 per diluted share, from $5.339 billion, or $7.14 per share. On a core basis, the loss was $0.34 per share, wider than the $0.21 loss analysts expected in the Zacks consensus, with Zacks putting revenue of $24.19 billion just below its $24.28 billion estimate.

"Recent milestones, including certification of the 737-7 and 737-10 and selection to design and build the Navy's sixth-generation fighter aircraft, are important steps as we continue building on our progress. But we are not done."

— Kelly Ortberg, Boeing president and CEO

Defense and Services Carry the Quarter

Commercial Airplanes remained the drag. Segment revenue fell 3% to $10.720 billion on a less favorable delivery mix, and the unit lost $697 million, a negative 6.5% margin, reflecting higher projected costs for future production rate adjustments and higher estimated supply chain costs. Boeing delivered 161 airplanes in the quarter — 124 of the 737 family, 22 of the 787, five 777s and 10 of the 767 — and booked 300 net orders, including from Turkish Airlines, Ethiopian Airlines and Lufthansa.

Defense, Space & Security did the heavy lifting on growth: revenue rose 15% to $7.935 billion and operating earnings rose to $492 million, a 6.2% margin that included a $252 million gain on the sale of HRL Laboratories. The Navy selected Boeing to design, build and deliver the F/A-XX next-generation fighter, though the award is not yet in backlog. Global Services revenue rose 4% to $5.574 billion with earnings of $1.019 billion, an 18.3% margin, and a US Army award to maintain the AH-64 Apache fleet.

Certification Wins, Production Still the Test

The quarter brought real program milestones. The 737-7 received amended type certification from the Federal Aviation Administration during the quarter, and the 737-10 was certified in October. The 787 held stable at eight aircraft per month, and 777-9 flight testing continued toward a first delivery in 2027. But the 737 line has not yet stabilized at 47 per month, a step now expected to take into next year.

Cash Flow and Backlog

Operating cash flow rose 33% to $1.496 billion and free cash flow was $464 million, even after roughly $700 million in Justice Department settlement payments. Cash and marketable securities rose to $20.7 billion, while consolidated debt was unchanged at $45.9 billion. Total backlog grew to a record $745 billion. On the earnings call, Boeing laid out a multi-year cash path of about $2 billion of free cash flow in 2026, rising toward $10 billion in 2029, while conceding it will fall short of its 500-jet delivery target for the year. The quarter confirmed the direction — losses narrowing, cash positive, backlog at a record — but the pace of the 737 ramp remains the number that decides the turnaround.
